x: Cascade is an animation library for Unity UI Toolkit. It animates any VisualElement at runtime with one line of C#: fades, moves, scales, colors, sizes, springs, staggered lists and screen transitions. It works with UXML/USS and UI Toolkit (UIElements) in Unity 6000.0 and later. It has no third-party dependencies and allocates nothing per frame. It doesn't support uGUI (Canvas). using Cascade; panel.Animate() .Fade(1f, 0.3f).From(0f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic) .MoveY(0f, 0.3f).From(24f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic); // both run together

Cascade comes in two tiers. Lite is free and MIT licensed, and covers the tween engine. Pro is a superset: it includes everything in Lite and adds the parts that are hard to write yourself. Add using Cascade; and call Animate() on any VisualElement. Durations are in seconds. using Cascade; using UnityEngine; using UnityEngine.UIElements; public class Intro : MonoBehaviour { void OnEnable() { var root = GetComponent<UIDocument>().rootVisualElement; var card = root.Q("card"); card.Animate() .Fade(1f, 0.3f).From(0f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic) .Then() .MoveY(0f, 0.4f).From(24f).Ease(Ease.OutBack); } } Verbs in the same step run together. Then() starts the next step after the current one finishes. From(v) sets where a verb starts. Without it, Cascade starts from the element's current value, so a card that is already visible has nothing to fade.

Animate() returns a handle you can keep: var pulse = badge.Animate().ScaleTo(1.15f, 0.5f).Ease(Ease.InOutSine).Loop(LoopMode.PingPong, 0); // 0 = forever pulse.Pause(); pulse.Resume(); pulse.Cancel(); // stops where it is badge.StopAnimations(); // stops everything on this element Cancelling leaves the element where it is and does not call OnComplete. An animation that finishes on its own snaps to its target and calls OnComplete. Animations also cancel themselves when the element leaves the panel, so nothing writes to a closed screen.

row.Animate().Fade(1f, 0.3f).OnSettled(completed => PaintSelection()); Use OnSettled for anything the player must see. It runs whether the animation finished or was cancelled. OnComplete doesn't run when a new animation replaces this one halfway, which happens whenever the player clicks quickly. Or await it. The result is true when it finished and false when it was cancelled: async void PlayIntro() { if (!await title.Animate().Fade(1f, 0.4f).From(0f)) return; // the screen closed: stop await subtitle.Animate().MoveY(0f, 0.35f).From(20f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic); }

h: How to animate a UI Toolkit VisualElement
x: Unity UI Toolkit has three built-in ways to animate a VisualElement at runtime: USS transitions, the panel scheduler, and the experimental animation API. They cover simple cases. For sequences, lists and interruptible motion, most projects end up writing their own tween layer or using a library. This page shows each option with working code and when to use it. Approach Good for Limits USS transitions hover and state changes styled in USS no sequencing, no completion callback beyond an event, needs a frame before it runs on a new element Panel scheduler one custom effect you write easing, timing, cancelling and cleanup yourself experimental.animation quick one-off tweens experimental API that can change between Unity versions; durations in milliseconds A tween library (Cascade) sequences, lists, springs, transitions a package to add

Declare which properties animate in USS, then change the element's class from C#. UI Toolkit animates between the two styles. .panel { opacity: 0; translate: 0 24px; transition-property: opacity, translate; transition-duration: 0.3s; transition-timing-function: ease-out-cubic; } .panel--open { opacity: 1; translate: 0 0; } panel.EnableInClassList("panel--open", true); This is the right tool for hover states and simple toggles, because the styling lives in USS with the rest of your look. Things to know: A class added in the same frame the element is created doesn't animate: the element has no previous style to animate from yet. Wait a frame, for example with panel.schedule.Execute(() => panel.AddToClassList("panel--open")). There's no built-in way to run step B after step A, or to start ten list items one after another. To react when it ends, register for TransitionEndEvent. It fires once per property; an interrupted transition sends TransitionCancelEvent instead.

Every element has a scheduler that runs code on the panel's update. You can drive any style value from it: void FadeIn(VisualElement el, float duration) { float start = Time.unscaledTime; IVisualElementScheduledItem item = null; item = el.schedule.Execute(() => { if (el.panel == null) { item.Pause(); return; } // the element left the screen float t = Mathf.Clamp01((Time.unscaledTime - start) / duration); float eased = 1f - Mathf.Pow(1f - t, 3f); // ease-out cubic el.style.opacity = eased; if (t >= 1f) item.Pause(); }).Every(0); } This gives you full control, and it's what most hand-written UI Toolkit tweening looks like. The cost is that every effect repeats the same work: easing, the start value, stopping a previous animation on the same element, and stopping when the element is removed. Most projects end up wrapping it in a small tween helper, which grows into a library over time.

UI Toolkit includes a small tween API under element.experimental.animation: using UnityEngine.UIElements.Experimental; el.experimental.animation .Start(new StyleValues { opacity = 0f }, new StyleValues { opacity = 1f }, 300) // milliseconds .Ease(Easing.OutCubic); It works for one-off tweens. It sits in the Experimental namespace, so it can change between Unity versions, and it has no sequencing, staggering or springs.

Cascade is a runtime animation library built for UI Toolkit. The same fade-and-rise as above is one call, and it handles the parts the scheduler version leaves to you: easing, start values, replacing an animation that's already running, and cancelling when the element leaves the panel. using Cascade; panel.Animate() .Fade(1f, 0.3f).From(0f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic) .MoveY(0f, 0.3f).From(24f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic); Sequences chain with Then(), and every animation can be awaited: await title.Animate().Fade(1f, 0.4f).From(0f); await button.Animate().ScaleTo(1f, 0.3f).From(0.8f).Ease(Ease.OutBack); Cascade Lite is free and MIT licensed, and covers everything on this page. Springs, staggered lists and screen transitions are in Pro. Get Cascade Lite (free) Getting started

A hover color or a toggle styled in USS: USS transitions. One unusual effect, such as a custom shader value: the scheduler, or Cascade's Value verb. Panels that slide in, then something else happens: a tween library, so the steps run in order and stop cleanly. Lists, interruptible buttons, screen changes: a library with stagger, springs and transitions. Animate translate, scale, rotate and opacity where you can. They don't trigger layout. Animating width, height, top or left re-runs layout every frame, which is fine for one accordion but slow for many elements.

Pro A spring moves an element toward its target like a physical object: it speeds up, can overshoot, and settles. Its length comes from its stiffness rather than a fixed duration. The real reason to use one is interruption. When a new target arrives halfway, a spring keeps its current speed and turns toward the new target. An eased tween has to start again from zero speed, which shows as a hitch. Anything the player can click rapidly, drag or toggle looks better on a spring. UI Toolkit has no spring animation built in: USS transitions and the experimental animation API only offer fixed-duration easing curves. Cascade Pro adds springs to every verb.

h: Add a spring to any verb
x: using Cascade; card.Animate().ScaleTo(1.2f, 0f).Spring(SpringPreset.Bouncy); panel.Animate().MoveY(0f, 0f).From(40f).Spring(SpringPreset.Snappy); Spring() replaces the verb's duration: the spring decides how long it takes, so pass 0f as the duration. Preset Feel Use for SpringPreset.Gentle slow, smooth, no visible bounce large panels, backgrounds SpringPreset.Snappy quick, settles fast buttons, menus, most UI SpringPreset.Bouncy overshoots and wobbles rewards, playful buttons, game UI

h: A custom spring, described by feel
x: Tuning stiffness and damping by hand is slow. SpringConfig.FromResponse takes two numbers that match what you see: // response: roughly how long one swing takes, in seconds (0.15 = a quick control, 0.5 = a large panel) // bounce: 0 = no overshoot, toward 1 = very bouncy var drawer = SpringConfig.FromResponse(0.4f, 0.15f); sidePanel.Animate().MoveX(0f, 0f).Spring(drawer); If you already know the physics values, use new SpringConfig(stiffness, damping, mass).

// Call this on every click. No StopAnimations() first, on purpose. void Flip() { _flip = !_flip; card.Animate().MoveX(_flip ? 90f : -90f, 0f).Spring(SpringPreset.Bouncy); } Click quickly and the card turns around smoothly instead of stopping dead each time. The animation that is replaced hands its current velocity to the new one. Call StopAnimations() first only when you want a hard reset, because it drops the velocity too.

playButton.OnHover().ScaleTo(1.12f, 0f).WithSpring(SpringPreset.Bouncy); playButton.OnPress().ScaleTo(0.94f, 0.08f); Moving the pointer on and off quickly keeps the motion continuous, for the same reason as above.

card.Animate() .MoveY(-40f, 0.3f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic) .Then().ScaleTo(1.1f, 0f).Spring(SpringPreset.Bouncy) .Then().MoveY(0f, 0f).Spring(SpringPreset.Snappy); A spring step ends when the spring has settled, then the next step starts.

h: When not to use a spring
x: Exact timing: a progress bar or something synced to audio needs a fixed duration. Use an ease. Fades: opacity has nothing to overshoot. An ease reads cleaner. Exits: things leaving the screen usually look better accelerating away with Ease.InCubic. Springs are in Cascade Pro. Cascade Lite (free) has the full easing set, including Ease.OutBack and Ease.OutElastic, which give an overshoot with a fixed duration. Get Cascade Pro

Pro A stagger plays the same animation on each item of a list, each one starting a little later than the one before. It makes a menu or a list of results read as one movement instead of a block appearing at once. using Cascade; using System.Linq; var items = listRoot.Query<VisualElement>(className: "row").ToList(); items.AnimateEach() .SlideIn(Edge.Right, 0.35f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic) .Fade(1f, 0.35f).From(0f) .Stagger(0.06f); // item i starts i × 0.06 s after the first AnimateEach() works on any list of VisualElements, so the result of a UQuery works directly. Write From(0f) on the fade. Each item starts from its own value when its turn comes, and an item that is already visible has nothing to fade. From also hides the later items right away, so they don't flash before their turn.

0.04–0.08 s per item works for most menus and lists. Above about 0.1 s a long list starts to feel slow. The whole group takes duration + (count − 1) × step, so it grows with the list. For lists whose length changes, fix the total time instead of the step: // spread the whole list over 0.4 s, but never more than 0.06 s between items float step = Stagger.StepForSpan(items.Count, 0.4f, 0.06f); items.AnimateEach().Fade(1f, 0.3f).From(0f).Stagger(step);
float total = Stagger.TotalDuration(items.Count, 0.35f, 0.06f); footer.Animate().Fade(1f, 0.25f).From(0f).Delay(total);

When the list is shown again, stop what is still running on the items first, so a quick re-open starts cleanly: foreach (var item in items) item.StopAnimations(); items.AnimateEach().SlideIn(Edge.Right, 0.35f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic).Fade(1f, 0.35f).From(0f).Stagger(0.06f);

Lite has no AnimateEach, but it has Delay. A loop gives the same result for a short list: for (int i = 0; i < items.Count; i++) { items[i].Animate() .Fade(1f, 0.3f).From(0f).Delay(i * 0.06f) .SlideIn(Edge.Right, 0.3f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic).Delay(i * 0.06f); } Pro's AnimateEach adds the timing helpers above, works with springs, and handles replays and cancelling for the whole group. Pro An enter/exit transition animates an element as it appears and disappears. The tricky part in UI Toolkit is display: an element must be display: flex before it can animate in, and should become display: none only after it has animated out, or it keeps taking space and catching clicks. Cascade Pro's Show and Hide handle that order for you. using Cascade; panel.Show(Transition.SlideFade(Edge.Bottom, 0.35f)); // display: flex, then animate in panel.Hide(Transition.ScaleFade(0.25f)); // animate out, then display: none

Transition Looks like Transition.Fade(d) opacity only Transition.Slide(edge, d) moves in from an edge Transition.SlideFade(edge, d) moves and fades; the usual choice for panels and toasts Transition.Scale(d) grows from 85% Transition.ScaleFade(d) grows and fades; the usual choice for dialogs Transition.Crossfade(d) a fade, used for swapping screens Add .WithEase(...) to any of them, for example Transition.ScaleFade(0.28f).WithEase(Ease.OutBack).

void ShowToast() { toast.StopAnimations(); // a second click restarts it cleanly toast.Show(Transition.SlideFade(Edge.Top, 0.3f).WithEase(Ease.OutCubic)); toast.schedule.Execute(HideToast).ExecuteLater(1900); } void HideToast() { if (toast.resolvedStyle.display == DisplayStyle.None) return; toast.Hide(Transition.SlideFade(Edge.Top, 0.25f).WithEase(Ease.InCubic)); } Ease out on the way in and ease in on the way out. Accelerating away reads as "dismissed".

h: Modal dialog with a dimmed backdrop
x: void OpenModal() { modalOpen = true; modalRoot.style.display = DisplayStyle.Flex; backdrop.Show(Transition.Fade(0.2f)); dialog.Show(Transition.ScaleFade(0.28f).WithEase(Ease.OutBack)); } void CloseModal() { modalOpen = false; backdrop.Hide(Transition.Fade(0.18f)); dialog.Hide(Transition.ScaleFade(0.2f)); // hide the container after the children finish, unless the modal was re-opened meanwhile modalRoot.schedule.Execute(() => { if (!modalOpen) modalRoot.style.display = DisplayStyle.None; }) .ExecuteLater(240); } Keep the backdrop on a plain fade and give the overshoot to the dialog, so only one thing draws the eye.

screens.SwapTo(settingsScreen, Transition.Crossfade(0.3f)); SwapTo animates the current child of screens out (ending at display: none) and the new one in. Both screens must already be children of screens.

void SwitchTab(int i) { if (i == current) return; // clicking the open tab does nothing pages[current].Hide(Transition.Fade(0.16f)); // out a little faster than in pages[i].Show(Transition.Fade(0.22f)); indicator.Animate().MoveX(tabs[i].layout.x, 0.28f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic); indicator.Animate().Width(tabs[i].layout.width, 0.28f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic); current = i; } Read layout only after the first layout pass, for example in a GeometryChangedEvent callback. Before that it returns zeros.

AnimateIn and AnimateOut play the same transitions but don't touch display. Use them when you manage visibility yourself. Anything that opens and closes repeatedly should use Show and Hide: an element left at display: none by a previous Hide stays invisible under AnimateIn.

Lite has no Show/Hide, but the same effect takes a few lines: // in panel.style.display = DisplayStyle.Flex; panel.Animate().SlideIn(Edge.Bottom, 0.35f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic).Fade(1f, 0.35f).From(0f); // out panel.Animate().Fade(0f, 0.25f).Ease(Ease.InCubic) .OnSettled(done => { if (done) panel.style.display = DisplayStyle.None; }); // "done" is false when a new animation replaced this one, e.g. the panel was opened again Get Cascade Pro Get Cascade Lite (free)
Short patterns for common UI, each one taken from the demo that ships with the package. Toasts, modals, tabs and screen swaps are on the transitions page, and lists on the stagger page.

Pro playButton.OnHover().ScaleTo(1.08f, 0.12f, Ease.OutBack); playButton.OnPress().ScaleTo(0.94f, 0.08f); playButton.OnFocus().ScaleTo(1.08f, 0.15f, Ease.OutBack); // keyboard and gamepad get the same feedback Declare these once when you set up the screen, not inside event handlers. Pair OnHover with OnFocus, or the feedback only works with a mouse.

void ToggleAccordion() { open = !open; body.Animate().Height(open ? 168f : 0f, 0.3f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic); } Give the body overflow: hidden in USS so its contents are clipped while it closes. Height re-runs layout every frame, which is what an accordion needs; for many elements at once, prefer MoveX, ScaleTo and Rotate, which don't.

Pro card.Variants() .State("normal", s => s.ScaleTo(1f).RotateTo(0f).FadeTo(1f).In(0.35f).WithSpring(SpringPreset.Snappy)) .State("featured", s => s.ScaleTo(1.2f).RotateTo(-5f).FadeTo(1f).In(0.35f).WithSpring(SpringPreset.Bouncy)) .State("dim", s => s.ScaleTo(0.9f).RotateTo(0f).FadeTo(0.4f).In(0.3f).With(Ease.OutCubic)); card.To("featured"); // later, from anywhere Declare each state once and move between them by name. Selection, difficulty pickers and inventory slots fit this well: three states cost three declarations, not a transition for every pair.

async void PlayIntro() { bool finished = await title.Animate().Fade(1f, 0.4f).From(0f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic); if (!finished) return; // cancelled: the screen closed, so stop here await subtitle.Animate().MoveY(0f, 0.35f).From(20f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic); await startButton.Animate().ScaleTo(1f, 0.3f).From(0.8f).Ease(Ease.OutBack); } Always check the result. An intro that continues after its screen has closed is a common source of errors. Await each animation once; keep the result if you need it again. Without async, Then() does the same and allocates nothing: card.Animate() .MoveY(-40f, 0.3f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic) .Then().MoveY(0f, 0.5f).Delay(0.6f).Ease(Ease.OutBounce); // rise, hold 0.6 s, fall

var pulse = badge.Animate().ScaleTo(1.15f, 0.5f).Ease(Ease.InOutSine).Loop(LoopMode.PingPong, 0); // 0 = forever spinner.Animate().Rotate(360f, 1f).Loop(LoopMode.Restart, 0); Keep the handle of a loop that runs forever. Without it, the only way to stop it is StopAnimations() on the element.

h: Bump something that is already moving
x: ship.Animate().MoveX(400f, 2f); // a long move ship.Animate().NudgeY(-12f, 0.15f); // a hit: adds a bump without stopping the move MoveX on an element that is already moving replaces that movement. Nudge, NudgeX and NudgeY add on top of it instead, which is what screen shake and hit reactions need.
int from = shown, to = coins; scoreLabel.Animate().Value(0f, 1f, 0.6f, t => scoreLabel.text = Mathf.RoundToInt(Mathf.Lerp(from, to, t)).ToString()) .Ease(Ease.OutCubic);

MotionSettings.Mode = MotionMode.Reduced; // Full, Reduced, Crossfade or None Set it once from your accessibility settings. Every animation started afterwards follows it: Reduced shortens and calms motion, Crossfade replaces movement with fades, and None jumps to the end values. Callbacks and await still complete, so game logic waiting on an animation keeps working. For motion that carries meaning, such as a loading spinner, opt out: spinner.Animate().Rotate(360f, 1f).Loop(LoopMode.Restart, 0).IgnoreReducedMotion();

Pro The UI Animator component lets designers add motion to a UI Toolkit screen from the Inspector: pick the elements, pick when, pick a preset, and preview it without entering Play mode.

The screen must be a UI Toolkit UI: a GameObject with a UIDocument component pointing at a UXML file. Give the elements you want to animate a name or a USS class in UI Builder, for example hero-card or menu-item.

Add the component. Select the GameObject with the UIDocument, then Add Component ▸ Cascade ▸ UI Animator. Add a rule. Click + in the Rules list. A rule reads as one sentence: these elements, on this trigger, play this. Choose the elements. Click the ▾ next to the selector. It lists every element name and USS class in your UXML, with how many elements each matches. Or type one: #hero-card targets one named element, .menu-item targets every element with that class. Choose when. OnEnable plays once when the screen appears (entrances). Hover, Press and Focus react to the pointer and keyboard. Choose what. Pick a preset with ▾, or choose Create New… to make one in place. Preview. Click ▶ on the rule. It plays in the Game view and then restores the elements. Adjust the preset and press ▶ again.

Presets are assets you reuse across screens and projects. Create them from Assets ▸ Create ▸ Cascade. Preset Use it for Contains Transition Preset entrances and exits fade, slide from an edge, scale; one duration; an ease or a spring Interaction Preset hover, press and focus scale, fade, rotate to an "active" look Sequence Preset multi-step choreography steps that run in order, each with actions that run together; every verb, each with its own timing, ease or spring A rule's Sequence slot wins over its simple preset. Name presets by intent, such as Entrance-SlideUp, Hover-Lift or Press-Squish, and keep them in one folder so the motion style travels with you.

When a selector matches several elements (such as .menu-item), set stagger on the rule: the seconds between each element's start. 0.06 gives the classic menu cascade. Stagger applies to OnEnable rules.

The Inspector warns about rules that would do nothing: an empty selector, a missing preset, a preset with no channels enabled, or a hover that only fades to full opacity (elements already rest there). No warnings means the rule will do something visible.

Nothing happens on ▶: the console says the selector matched nothing. Fix the name or class, or pick from the ▾ list. Nothing happens in Play mode: the preset changes nothing visible. Enable a channel. Hover doesn't react: live pointer input needs Play mode. ▶ previews the motion any time. An element is stuck halfway in edit mode: previews restore styles when they finish. If Unity was interrupted mid-preview, reopen the scene; edit-mode styles are never saved.
Connecting reduced motion to your settings menu: one line. Named states and screen swaps. Motion triggered by gameplay events. A developer can play any preset from code: myPreset.Play(element).
Pro UI Toolkit has no box-shadow. Cascade Pro adds a drop shadow and glow element drawn with a mesh, and on Unity 6.3 and later it animates the USS filter blur and tint.

DropShadowElement draws a soft shadow behind its children. Put the element you want shadowed inside it. using Cascade; var shadow = new DropShadowElement { shadowColor = new Color(0f, 0f, 0f, 0.5f), blur = 22f, // how far the edge fades, in pixels spread = 2f, // grows the shadow before the fade offsetY = 12f, // pushes it down, like light from above }; shadow.style.width = 110; shadow.style.height = 90; shadow.Add(card); It is also a UXML element, so you can add it to a layout in UI Builder and set its color, blur, spread and offsets there.

A glow is the same element with no offset and a bright color: var glow = new DropShadowElement { shadowColor = new Color(1f, 0.6f, 0.2f, 0.8f), blur = 18f, spread = 4f, offsetY = 0f }; glow.Add(rewardIcon); It's mesh-drawn: no shaders and any render pipeline. Each one costs an extra draw, which is fine for a few hero cards and buttons, not for every row of a long list.

Unity 6.3 added a filter property to UI Toolkit. Cascade animates two of its functions as verbs: background.Animate().BlurTo(8f, 0.3f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic); // blur radius in pixels icon.Animate().TintTo(new Color(1f, 0.4f, 0.4f), 0.2f); // flash red Other filter functions already on the element are kept. A filter re-renders the element every frame it animates, so measure it on your target devices. On Unity versions before 6.3 these verbs compile and do nothing, with a single console warning, so shared code stays portable.

UI Toolkit borrowed CSS from the web, and Cascade borrows its animation model from Framer Motion. If you know one, here is the other. Durations are seconds, like Framer Motion, not milliseconds like Unity's own scheduler. Verbs in one chain run together. .Then() starts the next step, where Framer Motion would use keyframes or a sequence. Animations stop when the element leaves the panel, the way Framer Motion stops on unmount. There is no layout animation (FLIP). The Width, Height, Top and Left verbs animate layout values directly.
What Cascade does every frame, what it costs, and what happens to an animation when the UI around it changes.

One scheduler tick per UI panel drives every animation on that panel. Cascade doesn't use Update(), coroutines or a MonoBehaviour. No per-frame garbage. Tweens are pooled and reused, and the update loop makes no allocations. The test suite checks this by measuring GC allocations while stepping many animations. Values are computed in plain C# and written to style. Cascade doesn't depend on Unity's experimental animation API. Animations run on unscaled time, so a paused game (Time.timeScale = 0) still animates its pause menu.

Verbs Property Cost Fade, MoveX/Y/To, Nudge, ScaleTo, Rotate, SlideIn opacity and transforms cheap: no layout BackgroundColor, TextColor colors cheap: repaint only Width, Height, Size, Top, Left layout re-runs layout each frame BlurTo, TintTo (Pro, Unity 6.3+) filter an extra render pass each frame Animate many elements with the cheap verbs. Use the layout verbs where the box really has to resize, such as an accordion. For very large groups, such as hundreds of grid cells, Pro's AnimateAll and StaggerFade run one shared animation for the whole group instead of one per element. See the API reference.

h: When the element leaves the screen
x: An animation cancels itself when its element is removed from the panel, for example when a screen closes or a list row is recycled. Cascade never writes to an element that is no longer displayed. A cancelled animation doesn't call OnComplete; OnSettled receives false, and await returns false.

h: Starting a new animation on a moving element
x: Each property is a channel: opacity, translate X, translate Y, scale, rotate, width, height, top, left. Starting a new animation on a channel replaces the one already running on it, from the current value, so there is no jump. Other channels keep going: a new fade doesn't stop a move. A replaced animation counts as cancelled, so it never calls OnComplete. Use OnSettled for anything that must happen either way. In Pro, a replaced spring hands its velocity to the new animation. Nudge, NudgeX and NudgeY don't claim a channel. They add on top of whatever is moving the element.

var h = el.Animate().Fade(1f, 0.3f); h.Cancel(); // this animation el.StopAnimations(); // everything on the element el.StopAnimations(MotionChannel.Opacity); // one property; the rest keeps going Stopping leaves the element where it is. An animation that reaches its end on its own snaps exactly to its target.

Debug.Log(MotionSettings.Stats); // active panels, sequences and tweens, plus pooled tweens MotionSettings.Stats is allocation-free. Show it on a debug overlay, or check in a test that animations really stopped.
Cascade is pure C# with no native code and no dependencies. It runs wherever UI Toolkit runs in Unity 6000.0 and later. Each release is tested in the editor and in a built standalone player.

An ease shapes the speed of an animation over its duration. Every curve below is in both Lite and Pro, under Ease. panel.Animate().MoveY(0f, 0.4f).From(24f).Ease(Ease.OutCubic);

h: Which Unity versions does Cascade support?
x: Unity 6000.0 and later. Each release is tested on the oldest supported version and on a current one. Animated blur and tint need Unity 6.3 or later; on older versions those two verbs do nothing.
No. Cascade animates UI Toolkit VisualElements only (UXML/USS, also called UIElements).

h: Does it work in the editor UI or only at runtime?
x: It's built for runtime UI: game menus, HUDs and app screens rendered by a UIDocument. The UI Animator component (Pro) also previews in edit mode.

h: What's the difference between Lite and Pro?
x: Lite is the free tween engine: every verb, easing, sequencing, loops, await and reduced motion. Pro adds springs, stagger, enter/exit and screen transitions, hover/press/focus, named states, the no-code UI Animator, JSON sequences, and shadow/glow. See the table on the overview.

h: How do I upgrade from Lite to Pro?
x: Remove Cascade Lite, then install Cascade Pro. Pro contains everything in Lite with the same namespace and calls, so your code keeps compiling. Don't install both at once.
Cascade Lite is MIT licensed. Cascade Pro uses the standard Unity Asset Store license.
All platforms UI Toolkit supports. Cascade is pure C# with no native code and no dependencies.

h: Why not just use USS transitions?
x: Use them for hover colors and simple toggles. They can't run steps in order, stagger a list, await the end, or spring. How to animate a VisualElement compares the options.
No. Tweens are pooled and the update loop is allocation-free; the test suite measures it. See Performance and lifecycle.

h: Does it keep animating when the game is paused?
x: Yes. Cascade runs on unscaled time, so a pause menu animates with Time.timeScale = 0.
The element is already at full opacity, so it fades from 1 to 1. Add .From(0f). More in Common mistakes.

h: Can an AI assistant write Cascade code?
x: Yes. Install the agent skill with npx skills add twitchedd/cascade-skill. See AI assistants and the skill.
